lines.text: The Strait of Malacca closes overnight. Which way do the oil tankers go now?
It's only a thought experiment, but look how thin this lane is: between Malaysia and the island of Sumatra, just 2.8 km wide at its narrowest.
And yet every day about 23.2M barrels of oil squeeze through it, 29% of all the oil that moves by sea.
It runs 900 km from end to end, the short cut from the oil fields of the Gulf to the factories of China, Japan and Korea.
Now rub it out. A tanker sailing east from India meets a wall of land, with Sumatra on one side and Malaysia on the other.
So where's the next door? The Sunda Strait, a gap between Sumatra and Java, far to the south.
Other tankers sail further still, through the Lombok Strait, east of Bali, and then north past Borneo.
Stranger still, Singapore, a port city at the narrow end of the lane, suddenly sits beside a blocked lane with no way through.
Because this one lane carries about 25% of all the goods the world trades, every one of those ships now takes the long way round.
Malacca or Hormuz: which closure would hurt the world more? Tell me below. Now picture it once more:
